transcript:
Header:
Date: 2027-09-25 15:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Patel (Redwood SE), Lena Torres (Zephyr CTO), Marcus Chen (Zephyr Head of ML), Sofia Ramirez (Zephyr Infra), Evan Park (Zephyr Product)

Summary: quick Optimize walkthrough focused on batching and prefix/KV cache recommendations plus a cost model example; customer interested in tradeoffs for high-throughput payments inference pipeline, VPC/private deployment constraints, and a benchmark run.

Topics: batching strategies, KV/prefix cache sizing, quantization tradeoffs, dedicated vs hosted, security (SOC2/KMS/audit), next steps for bench.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Jordan (Redwood): hey everyone good to see you, thanks for taking the time. we're gonna run through our Optimize recommendations — batching, kv/prefix caching, show a cost model example and then leave time for q&a
[00:18] Lena (Zephyr): hi all, quick note, we're particularly interested in lowering per-transaction token cost while keeping 95th latency under 200ms for our fraud detection scoring path
[00:30] Jordan: perfect, that's exactly what we'll try to map to. priya, want to kick off with batching basics?
[00:36] Priya (Redwood): yeah sure — so the main levers for token cost are batching, kv/prefix cache hit rate, and model selection/quantization. batching increases throughput by amortizing transformer kernel overhead — but it can add latency if you wait too long to fill a batch, so there's a sweet spot depending on arrival patterns
[01:02] Marcus (Zephyr): we're mostly real-time, spikes at 300 rps during peak and baseline 60 rps, median input length 120 tokens, tail up to 400 tokens. does that change your recommendations?
[01:18] Priya: okay that's helpful — with that profile you can use short-time-window batching (10-30ms wait) plus dynamic batch sizing; Redwood's runtime supports continuous batching so you don't need to fully buffer to a fixed batch size — we do micro-batching and priority routing so high-priority requests don't starve
[01:33] Jordan: real quick, when we say continuous batching: it forms batches across GPU workers and pipelines KV-caches; it helps keep latency low while getting batch efficiencies
[01:43] [small cross talk — mic noise] 
[01:50] Sofia (Zephyr): on the KV cache — can you explain prefix vs kv? we've seen 'prefix cache' in your docs, not fully sure how it maps to our conversational cache use case
[01:59] Priya: yeah, quick defs: prefix cache is caching repeated prompt prefixes or system context across requests — think of boilerplate system messages or user-profile context. KV cache refers to the key/value attention cache for autoregressive generation where we store past activations per token so subsequent tokens don't recompute. in practice when we say 'KV/prefix' cache in Optimize, we often mean a combined strategy: cache up to N tokens of prefix and reuse KV cache across similar requests, which can dramatically cut per-token compute
[02:32] Lena: hmm ok, for us many requests share the same instruction + customer profile chunk — so prefix caching seems valuable. what sort of hit rates can we expect?
[02:42] Priya: in payment flows where the prefix is stable across many requests, hit rates of 60-90% are realistic. we usually model baseline 50% in conservative cost models and then show upside sensitivity. the cost model we'll send includes a hit rate slider so you can see delta
[03:00] Jordan: this is a good point to show the example cost model from the deck — i'll describe the assumptions: model = open-q 13B quantized, tokens per request = 120 median, batch wait = 20ms, kv hit = 60% baseline, throughput target 300 rps peak. under those assumptions we estimate per-1M requests tco of X (we'll attach the spreadsheet)
[03:20] Marcus: when you say open-q 13B quantized, how much does quantization affect quality for our scoring model? false positives matter a lot
[03:28] Priya: quality impact depends on model and task; for short classification/scoring tasks quantization to 4-bit often has minimal KPI drift but we always recommend running evals against your labeled set — Redwood Optimize can run A/B evals or run a regression monitor to warn of drift
[03:46] Evan (Zephyr): timeline question — we need results in ~4 weeks to influence Q4 rollout. is that feasible?
[03:53] Jordan: yes on our side, typical pilot is 2-4 weeks: week 1 config + smoke, week 2 benchmarks, week 3 iterate on cache/batching, week 4 evaluation and docs. priya will run the bench with your traces
[04:10] [00:04:10] Priya: i'll also note that dedicated vs hosted is a decision point — dedicated gives predictable throughput and easier control of KV cache state if you want sticky workers, hosted is faster to stand up but might have multi-tenant tradeoffs around tail latency
[04:29] Sofia: we will likely want a VPC/private deployment for compliance. we need KMS controls and audit logs — do you support customer-managed keys?
[04:37] Jordan: yes, our Private offering supports customer KMS/HSM integrations and you can keep the control plane in your VPC. we also provide audit logs and can provide SOC2 compliance docs — we'll share the security appendix after the call
[04:53] Lena: any concerns about cold-start kv cache on scale-up? during spikes we fear a hit to latency if caches are cold
[05:01] Priya: good question — we recommend a combination: warm-up pools for expected spike windows and a small LRU cache on the serving side plus prewarming using historical prefixes. Redwood's routing can also route overflow requests to a slightly lower-cost variant to keep latency SLOs during cold start
[05:21] Marcus: can you explain the routing/fallback you mentioned? what do you mean by lower-cost variant?
[05:28] Jordan: e.g., have a smaller quantized model or lower-seq-length config as fallback; set a policy so when dedicated pool is saturated we route non-critical requests to fallback or to other regions. it's automated in the rollout config
[05:43] [00:05:43] Priya: i'll demo a quick graph — (screen share noise) — here's a sample cost curve: x-axis is KV hit rate from 0 to 100%, y-axis is per-million tokens cost. you can see steep savings as hit rate moves from 0 to 50%, then more linear beyond. batching gives step-wise improvements up to the point where you hit GPU saturation
[06:10] Jordan: also important is effective batch size distribution — tail latency matters: if you auto-batch a long-running request with short ones you'll amplify that long latency to others unless you do priority preemption
[06:22] Marcus: we have mixed lengths; could priority preemption under heavy load cause unfairness? we can't have core path starved
[06:29] Priya: you can configure classes — core scoring requests can be pinned to preemptive lanes; other non-critical tasks go to best-effort lanes. Redwood supports token-level cost tracking per route so you can see the economics per class
[06:44] [00:06:44] Sofia: on the infra side, what network egress or data residency concerns exist for a private deploy? we need traffic to stay in eu-west-1 and logs not to leave region
[06:55] Jordan: private deployments can be pinned to region and logs/audit retained in your cloud account; we'll work with your infra to ensure egress policies are enforced and we can disable external telemetry if required
[07:10] Marcus: about the benchmark run — what metrics will you capture? 95/99 latency, throughput, token cost breakdown?
[07:17] Priya: yes we'll capture p50/p95/p99 latency, avg tokens per request, cache hit rates, GPU utilization, and cost per token breakdown (compute, bandwidth, storage) — plus an experiments sheet showing sensitivity to kv hit and batch wait
[07:31] Evan: will you need sample PII data? we can't share raw card numbers but can we obfuscate traces?
[07:38] Jordan: completely fine — we typically accept anonymized traces or replay with synthetic tokens. Marcus: do you have a sample to share?
[07:45] Marcus: yes we can deliver a 24h trace with obfuscated identifiers
[07:49] Jordan: perfect, that will speed the bench setup
[07:52] [00:07:52] Priya: moving on — i want to call out a few practical configs: cache TTLs, cache sizes per worker, and eviction policy. for high throughput you size per-worker kv cache to hold the common prefix + expected max context window, but you also need to budget memory on GPU. the cost model ties memory footprint to GPU type and instance count
[08:15] Lena: do you have recommended GPU types for 13B quantized and heavy kv usage?
[08:22] Priya: A100 40GB is a common sweet spot; 80GB gives more headroom for larger kv caches. for 4-bit quantized 13B you can fit multiple workers per 40GB depending on sequence length; our tooling will recommend instance types given your target throughput and cache sizing
[08:38] Jordan: also we can show how batching + cache reduces the need for more GPUs — the cost model will show scenarios: no cache vs 50% hit vs 80% hit and the resulting GPU counts and monthly cost
[08:50] Marcus: any limitations around stateful KV cache at scale? i.e., can you maintain sticky KV cache across autoscaling events?
[08:58] Priya: autoscaling has two modes: stateless scale (fast) and stateful with sticky workers. for workloads needing persistent KV state we recommend dedicated pools with sticky worker assignment and controlled scale events, plus pre-warm strategies for new workers
[09:14] [00:09:14] Sofia: on security again — can we have role-based access control that limits who can change rollout policies? we need separation of duties
[09:21] Jordan: yes RBAC and SSO (SAML) are supported; you can lock down rollouts to a small admin group and give observers read-only dashboards
[09:30] Marcus: pricing structure question: hosted per-token vs dedicated reserved commitments — do you have a tipping point?
[09:36] Jordan: usual rule: if you have predictable sustained throughput, dedicated reserved capacity starts to make sense because unit costs drop. the cost model has a breakeven analysis where you plug in sustained rps and you can see commit level vs pay-as-you-go
[09:50] Evan: any vendor lock-in concerns? suppose we want to move models between cloud providers later
[09:55] Priya: Redwood abstracts model versions and runtime configs — you can pin model versions and move clusters between clouds but data movement is still your responsibility. we support exporting configs and images to help portability
[10:10] [00:10:10] Jordan: quick note on compliance: we maintain SOC2 and can provide ISO papers; for Fed/Risk customers we have private deployments and audit hooks (we'll attach the docs)
[10:20] Lena: question about function calling/structured outputs — our scoring pipeline sometimes needs deterministic outputs with schema — any gotchas with caching?
[10:28] Priya: prefix caching is safe if the deterministic portion is within the cached prefix; KV caching for autoreg generation is fine but we recommend strong post-output validation for any schema enforcement. also when you use cached prefix, ensure prompt tokens that change per-request are not inadvertently cached
[10:46] Marcus: ok let's talk numbers — can you show a sample per-request cost delta between no cache and 70% cache hit at 300 rps?
[10:55] Jordan: yes the spreadsheet has 3 scenarios — rough verbal numbers: no cache ~ $0.18/request, 50% cache ~ $0.11/request, 70% cache ~ $0.08/request (these are approx and depend on model and quantization). again we'll send the full calc with GPU pricing broken out
[11:14] [00:11:14] Evan: those deltas are promising. any impact to model update/rollouts when using prefix caching?
[11:20] Priya: when you roll a model you can invalidate caches or run gradual rollouts; Redwood's rollout tool lets you flush prefix caches by route or tag and do canary runs so you catch regressions before full cutover
[11:35] Sofia: can we measure cache hit rate in real-time? need that for ops dashboards
[11:40] Jordan: yes, the Console exposes per-route cache hit, avg batch size, and token-level cost; you can set alerts for hit-rate drops
[11:48] Marcus: any pitfalls with synthetic workloads vs real traffic during bench? we get different batch distributions in synthetic load
[11:55] Priya: totally — synthetic is okay for rough numbers but real traces are best for batching behavior; if you can't share traces, try to mirror arrival distribution (poisson vs bursty) and token length distribution
[12:09] [00:12:09] Jordan: let's go through a short example config for your scoring route — route = /score, priority = high, batch_wait = 20ms, max_batch = 128, cache_prefix_size = 256 tokens, cache_ttl = 10m, fallback_route = /score-fast (smaller model)
[12:29] Marcus: is cache_ttl per user or global?
[12:32] Priya: TTL semantics are per cache key — usually per prefix key + user id if you include that. for your case with common prefixes you'll probably key on customer_profile_id + route
[12:44] Lena: any guidance on eviction policy? lru vs ttl-only?
[12:48] Priya: LRU with TTL is common; TTL ensures stale contexts expire while LRU handles memory pressure. also monitor cache churn metric -- high churn suggests you need larger cache or different keying
[12:59] [00:12:59] Jordan: switching to slide on autoscale costs — autoscaling based on queue length vs rps gives different GPU counts; with heavy cache hits you can sustain higher rps per GPU so autoscale thresholds can be more aggressive
[13:15] Evan: ok question from product — if we need deterministic scoring for audit, how do you capture audit trail?
[13:22] Jordan: we persist input, model version, config, and model logits if needed (configurable) to your S3/secure bucket; logs are time-stamped and you can tie them to the request id for replay
[13:35] Marcus: hypothetically, if we do a private deploy and use KMS, who holds the keys? we need customer-held keys ideally
[13:42] Jordan: customer-held KMS is supported in Private; Redwood can integrate with your KMS/HSM and never store plaintext keys in our control plane
[13:49] [00:13:49] Priya: a couple of nitty-gritty performance tips: 1) avoid mixing long-context generation with short scoring in same route; 2) use separate lanes and model versions; 3) measure effective batch size distribution not just average, because tails will eat latency
[14:07] Lena: if we separate lanes is there extra cost?
[14:11] Priya: slightly more overhead if you provision separate pools but it protects latency. sometimes it's cheaper to have a small dedicated pool for high-priority requests and a larger best-effort pool for the rest
[14:24] Marcus: any DB or state requirements for prefix cache invalidation? we have user profile updates that should invalidate cached prefixes quickly
[14:33] Priya: you can hook your profile update event (webhook) to our cache invalidation API; it's a small call that evicts keys by id so changes propagate quickly
[14:42] [00:14:42] Jordan: ok let's surface risks and tradeoffs quickly: caching greatly reduces compute cost but increases operational complexity (cache sizing, invalidation). batching reduces unit cost but requires tuning to meet latency SLOs. dedicated gives predictability but requires commit. Those are the knobs
[14:59] Evan: thanks — i think the tradeoffs are clear. one more Q: are there any regulatory pitfalls with storing KV cache? e.g., if the prefix contains PII?
[15:08] Priya: we recommend avoiding storing raw PII in caches; if you must, encryption at rest and strict key rotation & short TTLs help. best practice: tokenize or obfuscate sensitive fields before caching
[15:20] Marcus: got it. ok can we confirm the deliverables and timeline?
[15:24] Jordan: yes, recap of next steps: jordan sends the cost spreadsheet and security appendix by 10/1; priya runs bench week of 10/4; customer provides traces and SLOs by 10/1; we reconvene after bench to review results
[15:38] Lena: perfect, thanks everyone. any final comments?
[15:42] Priya: i'll follow up with an invite for the benchmark kickoff and include the test plan; expect the bench to take 2-3 days of running plus analysis
[15:50] Jordan: thanks folks — we'll also include an example rollout config and a short README for prefix cache keying
[15:56] [00:15:56] Evan: great talk, thanks Redwood team
[16:00] Jordan: thanks Zephyr, talk soon
